common_name: Hokie Pink Summersweet (Large Deep-Pink Native Clethra)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Hokie Pink, a Virginia Tech introduction, grows into a larger plant than Ruby Spice, useful where a bigger fragrant summer-blooming shrub is wanted.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade, keeping soil consistently moist since summersweet does not tolerate extended drought. Hokie Pink, introduced by Virginia Tech, bears the same deeply fragrant, upright bottlebrush flower spikes as other pink summersweet cultivars, in a rich rose-pink, but on a notably larger, more vigorous shrub than the more commonly planted Ruby Spice — a strong choice where a taller fragrant screen or backdrop planting is wanted rather than a compact specimen. Its midsummer bloom period draws heavy bee, butterfly, and hummingbird moth traffic during a season when many other shrubs have finished flowering, and the glossy foliage turns clear yellow in fall. Suckers slowly to form a broad colony over time, useful for naturalizing in a moist, partly shaded border or woodland edge.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Virginia Tech Hampton Roads Agricultural Research and Extension Center

common_name: Densa Walter's Viburnum (Dense Compact Native Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Densa forms a naturally tight, rounded mound, useful for a low hedge or mass planting with minimal shearing.

directions: Densa is a compact, tightly branched selection of native Walter's viburnum forming a dense, fine-textured, rounded mound of small, glossy, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves, holding its neat shape with far less shearing than the straight species. Clusters of small white flowers open in spring, followed by small fruit that ripens through red to black and draws songbirds, on a plant scaled for foundation plantings, informal hedges, and mass groupings in a partly shaded to sunny border. Like other Walter's viburnum selections it adapts to a range of soil moisture, from average garden conditions to occasionally wet sites, and tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf South summers with ease. Light shaping after spring bloom is usually all the maintenance it needs to stay dense and tidy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Viburnum obovatum Cultivars
Florida Native Plant Society — Walter's Viburnum
North Carolina State Extension — Native Viburnum Selection

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; BananAppeal stays more compact than the straight species, fitting a foundation bed or hedge where the full-sized yellow anise would grow too large.

directions: BananAppeal is a more compact selection of small anise tree, keeping the species' bright lime-green, glossy evergreen foliage and dense, screening habit in a smaller package better suited to a foundation planting, hedge, or shaded border than the full-sized species, which can reach well over 10 feet. Crushing or brushing against the aromatic leaves releases the distinctive sweet, fruity fragrance that gives the plant its name. Tiny, inconspicuous pale yellow flowers appear in spring, but the plant is grown almost entirely for its dense, shade-tolerant evergreen structure. Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade, where it thrives in the difficult wet, shaded conditions that challenge many broadleaf evergreens, and needs only light shaping to maintain a tidy form.

common_name: Zhuzhou Fuchsia Loropetalum (Vigorous Deep Fuchsia-Pink Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Zhuzhou Fuchsia grows into a large, vigorous shrub and is often used as a small flowering tree or tall privacy screen rather than a compact foundation plant.

directions: Zhuzhou Fuchsia is one of the original large-growing purple-leaf loropetalum introductions, valued for exceptionally vivid, deep fuchsia-pink fringe flowers set against burgundy-purple new foliage that matures to a darker bronze-green. Unlike the many compact loropetalum cultivars bred since its introduction, Zhuzhou Fuchsia grows quickly into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small specimen tree, making it a strong choice for a tall privacy screen, background planting, or trained standard rather than a tight foundation bed. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic soil in full sun to partial shade — more sun deepens the foliage color, while some shade tempers growth rate. It blooms heaviest in spring with lighter repeat flushes through the growing season, and tolerates Gulf South heat and humidity with very few pest or disease problems. Prune, if needed, right after the spring flush to shape without removing the next round of buds.

common_name: Carolina Panther Loropetalum (Near-Black Foliage Compact Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina Panther holds some of the darkest foliage color available in the genus, with 4-6 hours of direct sun giving the deepest color.

directions: Carolina Panther, a North Carolina State University introduction, is prized for foliage so dark it reads as near-black in good light, among the deepest coloring available in the loropetalum genus, contrasting sharply with bright magenta-pink fringe flowers that open heaviest in spring with lighter repeat bloom through the growing season. Its moderate, well-branched size fits foundation plantings and mixed borders without the size management larger loropetalum cultivars require. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; more direct sun intensifies the foliage's dark coloring, while deeper shade shifts the leaves toward a more ordinary green-bronze. Loropetalum is generally trouble-free in Gulf South heat and humidity, and light pruning right after spring bloom is enough to keep the shape tidy without sacrificing the next flush of flowers.
sources: North Carolina State University JC Raulston Arboretum
